transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess what finally got me in here is this memorial I’ve been putting together for my brother. It started out as a simple thing, you know, just honoring him properly, maybe some music he liked, a few photos, people saying a few words. But it’s gotten… bigger. A lot bigger than I meant it to.

Most days now I’m chasing down songs, calling people, figuring out displays, thinking about trips connected to it, trying to make sure every piece is just right. I’ll start in the morning and then suddenly the whole day’s gone. My wife keeps telling me I’ve pushed aside the garden, my walking group, and just about everything else I used to do. I don’t know, I feel like it matters, but she thinks I’ve gotten too wrapped up in it.
Do you feel like the memorial has to be perfect?

Perfect… I don’t know if I’d use that word exactly, but it does feel like every piece has to be right, if that makes sense. It started as just a memorial for my brother, something simple and decent, but then I keep thinking of one more song he loved, one more person I should call, one more photo or display that would explain who he was better.

And then I’ll think, well, maybe there should be a trip connected to it, or some place that meant something to him, and suddenly I’m spending the whole day on it. My wife says I’ve let the garden go, and I haven’t been keeping up with the walking group or much of anything else. I don’t mean for it to take over like that, but once I get started, it feels important to keep pushing until it all comes together the right way.
Do you feel anxious or uncomfortable when you think about not being able to include every detail you want in the memorial?

I’m not sure I’d call it anxious, exactly. Maybe uncomfortable, yes, but it’s hard for me to separate that from just feeling like I’m not doing right by him. If I think, “Well, leave that song out,” or “Maybe don’t call that person,” I start going over it in my head, like maybe that was the one thing that would’ve mattered, or the one person who should’ve been included.

But I don’t know if it’s fear the way you mean it. It’s more like… I keep thinking there’s a better version of it, and if I stop too soon then I’ll have missed something important. My wife says I’m making too much of every little detail, and maybe I am, but when it’s my brother, it doesn’t feel little to me.
Do you feel like you need to be in charge of every aspect of the memorial?

I don’t know if I’d say I need to be in charge of every single part. I mean, people can help, and my wife has tried, and I’m not against that in principle. It’s just that when someone else suggests something, I start thinking, well, they didn’t know him the way I did, or they might miss why a certain song matters, or why a certain photo should go next to another one.

So I guess I do end up holding onto a lot of it myself. Not because I’m trying to boss everyone around, at least I don’t think so. It’s more that I feel like I’m the one who understands what it’s supposed to mean. But then again, maybe that does come across like I have to run the whole thing. My wife would probably say yes to that question faster than I would.
Do you think something bad would happen if the memorial wasn't done exactly as you envision it?

Yes… I mean, I know how it sounds when I say it out loud, but yes, in a way I do. Not like the chairs being crooked would make the roof fall in or anything like that. It’s more… there are things in those old ballads my brother kept, the ones he loved, and I’ve listened to them over and over now. I’m certain there are warnings tucked into the words. Not just lyrics, not just old sad songs.

My wife says I’m reading too much into it, that I’m hearing what I want to hear because I miss him, but I know what I heard. Certain lines stand out, like they’re meant for me, like they’re telling me not to leave something out or not to put things in the wrong order. So if the memorial isn’t done the way it’s supposed to be done, the way I’m seeing it in my head, then yes, I do worry something bad could come from ignoring that. I can’t prove it to you neatly, I know that, but it feels very clear to me.
Do you think other people would hear those warnings in the ballads if they listened to them the way you have?

I think they could, if they really listened. Not just had it playing in the background while they were washing dishes or something, but sat with it the way I have, listened to the words, the pauses, the way certain lines come back around. I know that probably sounds strange, but I’m not just making it up out of thin air.

My wife says I’m reading too much into it, and maybe other people would say the same thing at first. But I know what I heard. Those old ballads my brother kept, they’re not just songs to me now. There are warnings tucked into them, like certain words are meant to point me toward what I’m supposed to do for him. Maybe not everyone would catch it right away, because they didn’t know him and they haven’t listened over and over like I have. But if they listened the right way, I think they’d hear at least some of it.
Do you think these warnings in the ballads are meant for anyone else besides you?

Mostly me. That’s the honest answer. I don’t think they’re, you know, broadcasting to everyone like some announcement on the radio. It feels more particular than that. They were my brother’s ballads, the ones he kept, the ones he went back to, and now when I listen to them, certain lines don’t just sound like lyrics anymore. They feel aimed at me.

I know that sounds odd. I can hear myself saying it, and I know my wife would shake her head and say I’m reading too much into it again. But I still know what I heard in those words. It’s like there are warnings tucked inside them, and they’re warning me about what I’m supposed to do, how I’m supposed to handle the memorial, what not to leave out.

Maybe someone else could understand parts of it if they were close enough to him, or if they listened carefully enough, but I don’t think it’s really meant for just anybody. It feels like it was left for me to catch.
Do you think you could be wrong about the warnings you hear in the ballads?

I suppose anybody could be wrong about anything, if you put it that way. I’m not trying to say I’m some perfect judge of every little thing. I know grief can do things to a person, and I know my wife thinks that’s what this is, that I’m taking these old songs my brother kept and turning them into something they’re not.

But when I actually sit there and listen—really listen—it doesn’t feel like a mistake. It feels very clear. Those ballads aren’t just songs to me now. There are warnings tucked into them, certain words and lines that stand out like they’re meant for me. And even when I try to tell myself, “Maybe she’s right, maybe you’re reading too much into it,” I still come back to the same thing: I know what I heard.

So could I be wrong? I guess, in a plain common-sense way, yes, maybe. But I don’t feel wrong about it. I feel certain enough that I can’t just ignore it.
Would you consider changing your plans for the memorial if someone you trust, like a close friend or family member, listened to the ballads and didn't hear the warnings you do?

I’d listen to them, yes. I mean, if it was someone I really trusted, I wouldn’t just brush them off. If my wife sat down with me, or someone who knew my brother well, and they said, “I don’t hear what you’re hearing,” I’d try to take that in.

But changing the memorial plans… that’s harder. Because it isn’t just that I’m hearing a sad song and making it fit. I know it sounds odd when I say it out loud, but those old ballads he kept, they don’t feel like ordinary songs anymore. There are words in them, certain lines, that land in a way that feels like a warning. Like they’re meant for me to notice. And my wife has already told me I’m reading too much into it, more than once, but that doesn’t make what I heard go away.

So if someone else didn’t hear it, I might think, well, maybe they’re not listening the same way, or maybe they don’t have the same connection to him. I don’t mean that in an arrogant way. It’s just… I’ve spent time with those songs. I’ve heard the warnings in them. I know what I heard.

I might make small adjustments if people were upset or if they thought something would embarrass the family, but I don’t think I could just ignore the warnings altogether. Not just because someone else didn’t pick up on them. That would feel like turning my back on something I was supposed to understand.
Would you still believe you hear warnings in the ballads if everyone you trust told you they don't hear them?

I think… yes. I don’t say that to be stubborn, and I don’t mean I wouldn’t care what they thought. If everyone I trusted sat me down and said, “We don’t hear any warnings in those songs,” that would shake me. I’d probably feel embarrassed, maybe defensive, and I’d wonder if I was somehow hearing it differently because it was my brother and because those were his old ballads.

But even then, I don’t think it would make me stop believing it. Not completely. Because when I listen to them, it isn’t vague to me. It’s not just a mood or me saying, “Oh, this song reminds me of him.” Certain words catch, certain lines feel placed there, almost tucked inside the music for me to notice. I know it sounds odd. I can hear that. But I’m certain those old ballads he kept aren’t just songs now. They’ve got warnings in them for me.

My wife has already told me I’m reading too much into it, and I’ve tried to take that seriously. I really have. But her saying that doesn’t change what I heard in those words. So if everyone said the same thing, I might get quieter about it, maybe keep more of it to myself, but inside I think I’d still know what I heard.
Do you think the warnings you hear in the ballads could be a product of your own mind rather than actual messages?

I’ve tried to ask myself that, honestly. I’m not completely closed off to the idea that my mind could be… shaping things, I suppose. I know after losing my brother, and with everything tied up in those old ballads he kept, a person can start noticing things they might not have noticed before.

But when you ask if it could just be coming from my own mind, that’s where I get stuck. Because when I listen to them, it doesn’t feel like I’m inventing it. It feels like the warnings are already there, tucked into the words, and I’m just finally hearing them properly. Certain lines stand out in a way I can’t explain away. It’s not like I sat there wanting to find a message and then forced one into the song.

My wife says I’m reading too much into it, and I understand why she says that. If I were listening to someone else say this, maybe I’d think it sounded strange too. But knowing it sounds odd doesn’t make it feel any less real to me. I still know what I heard in those words. So could my mind be part of it? Maybe, in some way. But I don’t believe it’s only my mind. I’m certain those ballads aren’t just songs. They’ve got warnings in them for me.
Do you think there's any possibility that the warnings you hear in the ballads are not real?

I suppose if I’m being fair, I can say there’s a possibility. I mean, I know how it sounds when I describe it. I’m not deaf to that. If someone else told me, “There are warnings hidden in these old ballads,” I might wonder if grief was making them hear things in a certain way.

But for me, sitting there with those songs my brother kept, listening to the words over and over… it doesn’t feel unreal. It doesn’t feel like I’m making it up. Certain lines just hit differently, like they’re not only lyrics anymore, like they were meant to be noticed by me. That’s the part I can’t get away from.

My wife says I’m reading too much into it, and I try to respect that because she’s not trying to hurt me. She’s worried, I think. But even when she says that, I still know what I heard in those words. So yes, maybe there’s some small possibility I’m wrong, but I don’t really believe the warnings are not real. I’m still pretty certain those ballads aren’t just songs. They’ve got warnings tucked inside them for me.
Do you think the warnings in the ballads would still be there if you weren't listening to them?

Yes… I think they would. That’s the strange part, I suppose. It doesn’t feel like the warnings only exist because I happen to be listening at that moment, like I’m creating them while the song plays. It feels more like they’re already in there, tucked into the ballads, whether I have them on or not.

I know that probably sounds odd. I can hear myself saying it, and I know my wife would say, “You’re reading too much into it.” She has said that. But to me, those old ballads my brother kept aren’t just songs anymore. The words are carrying something. When I listen, I’m not putting the warning there — I’m noticing what’s already there.

So if I wasn’t listening, I suppose I wouldn’t be hearing them right then, obviously. But that doesn’t mean the warnings disappear. They’d still be in the songs, waiting, in a way. And when I go back and play them again, certain lines catch the same way, like they were meant for me to hear. That’s why it’s hard for me to dismiss it. I still know what I heard in those words.
Do you think the warnings in the ballads would still make sense to you if your brother was alive and told you there were no hidden messages in them?

If my brother were alive and he sat right in front of me and said, “No, there are no hidden messages in those songs,” I’d want to believe him. I really would. He knew those ballads better than anyone, and they were his, in a way. I’d listen to him. I wouldn’t just brush him off.

But… I don’t know that it would make the warnings stop making sense to me. That’s the hard part. Because what I hear in them doesn’t feel like something I decided on because he died, or because someone told me to look for it. It feels like the words themselves are carrying it. Like the warnings are tucked in there, whether anyone else admits it or not.

Maybe I’d think he was trying to protect me, or maybe he didn’t hear them the same way I do. I know that sounds odd. I can hear that it sounds odd even as I’m saying it. My wife says I’m reading too much into it, and maybe my brother would say the same thing if he were here. But even then… I’d still know what I heard in those words.

So yes, I suppose it would shake me some if he said that. I’d be upset, probably confused. But I don’t think it would make me believe the ballads are just songs. Not completely. I’m certain there are warnings in them for me.
Do you think anyone else could hear the warnings in the ballads if they didn't know your brother or his story?

I think… yes and no. If they didn’t know my brother, or what happened, maybe they wouldn’t catch it the same way I do. They might just hear an old ballad and think it’s sad, or pretty, or strange, and then move on. I understand that. I know not everybody would sit with the words the way I have.

But that doesn’t mean the warnings aren’t there. That’s the part I keep trying to explain. It’s not like I’m inventing them out of nowhere. They’re tucked into the words, into certain lines, the way the songs turn. I know it sounds odd, and I know my wife says I’m reading too much into it, but when I hear them, I know what I heard.

Maybe someone else could hear them if they listened carefully enough. Maybe they wouldn’t need to know my brother’s whole story, but they’d have to be paying attention in the right way. Still, I do think they’re meant for me more than for just anyone. Those were his ballads, and when I listen now, they’re not just songs. They’ve got warnings in them, and I can’t make myself believe otherwise.
Do you think the warnings in the ballads would still be real if everyone, including mental health professionals, told you they are just a product of your grief and not actual messages?

I know what you’re asking. If everybody — my wife, you, other doctors, anyone I trusted — said, “This is grief, this is your mind making meaning because you miss your brother,” I suppose I’d have to sit with that. I’m not trying to be stubborn just to be stubborn. I can hear how it sounds when I say the songs have warnings in them. I do know it sounds odd.

But even if everyone said that, I don’t think it would make them stop feeling real to me. That’s the honest answer. Because when I listen to those old ballads he kept, it isn’t just a sad feeling or memories coming up. Certain words catch, certain lines feel like they’re pointing at something, like they’re meant for me. It doesn’t feel like I’m just putting it there afterward.

My wife says I’m reading too much into it, and maybe professionals would say the same in a more medical way, that it’s grief or my mind trying to connect things. I can understand the explanation, I really can. But understanding that other people see it that way doesn’t erase what I heard. I still know what I heard in those words.

So… yes, I’d probably feel confused, maybe embarrassed, maybe even a little angry if everyone dismissed it. But deep down, I’d still believe the ballads aren’t just songs. They’ve got warnings tucked inside them for me.
Do you think the warnings in the ballads would still exist if nobody else in the world believed they were there?

If nobody else in the world believed they were there… I think they’d still exist. That’s what’s difficult to say out loud, because I know how it makes me sound. It makes me sound like I’m putting myself against everyone else, and I don’t want to be that kind of man. I’m not trying to be unreasonable.

But when I hear those old ballads my brother kept, they aren’t just songs to me. They’re not just melodies and old words. There are warnings tucked inside them — in the phrasing, in certain lines, in the way the words land. I don’t know how to explain it so it makes sense to you the way it makes sense in my head, but I know what I heard.

My wife tells me I’m reading too much into it, and maybe if everyone said that, I’d feel ashamed or lonely with it. I might stop talking about it so much. But stopping talking about it wouldn’t mean I stopped knowing it. Even if not one other person believed me, I’d still feel certain the warnings are there, and that they’re meant for me.
Do you think the warnings in the ballads would still be real even if there was concrete evidence proving they are just a product of your imagination?

Concrete evidence… that’s a hard thing for me to answer, because part of me wants to say, well, if it was truly concrete, then I’d have to accept it, wouldn’t I? I’m not an educated man in the way doctors are, but I’m not trying to ignore facts just for the sake of it. I do understand what evidence means.

But then when I think about the ballads themselves — those old songs my brother kept, the words he held onto — it doesn’t feel like something that can be measured in that way. That’s where I get stuck. You could show me papers, or explain how grief works, or say my mind is filling in meanings that aren’t really there, and I might nod along because I can see how that sounds reasonable from the outside.

But when I hear those lines, when certain words come up, it lands in me like a warning. Not just sadness. Not just memory. It feels like something tucked inside the song, something meant for me to notice. And I know that sounds odd. I know my wife thinks I’m reading far too much into it, and maybe you’d say the same in a more professional way. But I still know what I heard in those words.

So if you’re asking whether evidence would make the warnings stop feeling real… I don’t think it would, not completely. Maybe it would make me doubt myself for a while, maybe feel ashamed or confused. But deep down, I’d still believe those ballads aren’t just songs. I’d still feel certain there are warnings in them for me.
Do you think the warnings in the ballads would still be real if a recording of your brother's voice, made before he passed away, explicitly stated that there are no hidden messages in those songs?

If it was his voice… my brother’s actual voice, recorded before he passed, saying plain as day, “There are no hidden messages in those songs,” I won’t pretend that wouldn’t shake me. It would. I’d probably sit there and listen to it over and over, because hearing him say it would mean something to me. He’s the one who kept those ballads, so if he said that, I’d have to take it seriously.

But I don’t think it would settle it the way you might expect. That’s the part I know sounds strange. Because what I hear in those songs doesn’t feel like just something he deliberately planted there, like a code he wrote down and could later deny. It feels more like the warnings are tucked into the words themselves, in the old lines, in the way they come through when I listen. Certain phrases just catch me. They land wrong, or maybe right — like they’re meant for me.

So if his recording said there were no hidden messages, I’d be torn. I’d feel guilty, honestly, like I was going against him by not fully accepting it. And my wife would probably say, “See, that proves you’re reading too much into it.” Maybe you’d say the same. And I can understand that. I really can.

But even then… I think I’d still know what I heard. I know it sounds odd, but those old ballads aren’t just songs to me. There are warnings in them, and they feel meant for me, even if nobody else — even his own voice — said they weren’t there.
Do you think your belief in the warnings in the ballads would change if you received professional help for your grief?

I think help with my grief might help me carry it better, if that makes sense. Maybe I wouldn’t feel so raw when I hear my brother’s songs, or maybe I wouldn’t sit with them for hours turning every line over in my head. I can see how talking to someone might make the hurt less sharp.

But I don’t know that it would change what’s in the ballads. That’s the part I keep coming back to. I know it sounds odd — I do know that — but those old ballads my brother kept aren’t just songs to me. There are warnings tucked into them. It’s in certain words, certain lines, the way they seem to come forward when I hear them. It feels directed at me, like I’m supposed to notice.

My wife says I’m reading too much into it, and maybe grief does make a man look harder at things. I’m willing to admit that. But even when I try to step back and tell myself, “Maybe this is just sorrow talking,” I still know what I heard in those words. So professional help might change how upset I get about it, maybe, but I don’t think it would make the warnings stop being real to me.
